text: Why is photon loss called the 'easy' error for dual-rail photonic qubits?
choices: Because lost photons are automatically replaced by the vacuum port
Because loss never actually affects the computation
Because in dual rail both |0>_L and |1>_L carry exactly one photon, so a loss leaves vacuum, a located (heralded) erasure whose correction thresholds far exceed those of unlocated Pauli errors
Because photon loss is a Pauli-X error that is trivial to correct
explanation: Since both logical states carry one photon, losing it yields detectable vacuum, a located erasure, and erasure thresholds (~50% on the surface code) dwarf Pauli thresholds (~11%). Loss is not auto-replaced (choice 0), does affect the qubit (choice 1), and is an erasure rather than a Pauli-X error (choice 3).
